name: Water hardness vs the hard-water threshold
title: Water hardness in {city}, {SS}
alt: Chart comparing water hardness in {city}, {SS} against the threshold for hard water. {summary}

research.ask: "water_hardness_gpg" — the average hardness of the municipal water supply serving {city}, {SS}, in GRAINS PER GALLON as a plain number (divide ppm or mg/L by 17.1 if the published figure is in those units). Use the figure published by the local water utility or a state/USGS survey. Omit this field rather than estimating: a plausible-looking hardness figure with a citation attached is worse than no figure at all.
research.source_ask: "water_hardness_source" — name the SPECIFIC published document this figure came from: the water utility's own annual water quality report (give the utility name and the report year), or a named USGS dataset. Do not answer with a generic organisation name. If you cannot identify a specific published figure for this city's municipal supply, omit water_hardness_gpg entirely.

captions: Water serving {city}, {SS} measures {self_value}; water is classified hard from {benchmark_value}. {difference} Dissolved mineral comes out of solution on heating elements and valves, so hardness decides how fast scale builds in a dishwasher, washing machine or water heater.

{city} water runs at {self_value}. {difference} Scale insulates a heating element, so it runs hotter and longer for the same result — the ordinary route to a burnt-out element, and the reason two identical machines can fail years apart in different towns.

{difference} At {self_value}, the supply to {city} sits against a classification threshold of {benchmark_value}. Every gallon leaves a little mineral behind in valves, seals and spray arms, and how much it leaves is set by the water rather than the machine.
_note: NOT converted to fetch, and a regional AI-ask tier was tried and reverted (2026-10-05). The USGS/EPA Water Quality Portal does return hardness samples by county FIPS (1,415 for Angelina County TX), but they mix surface water and groundwater and ranged 1-614 mg/L there, so a county median is not the municipal supply figure this chart claims. A second research tier asking for a named regional USGS/state groundwater classification was added, tried on appliance-site, and only lifted coverage from 5/100 to 13/100 (the model applied the same caution one level up, declining unless it knew a specific-enough regional study) — not worth the added cost/complexity for that yield, reverted to city-specific-only. A groundwater-only county-level fetch (filtered by site type) is technically possible via the WQP API, but is only valid for cities whose municipal supply actually IS groundwater — a surface-water city's well data is irrelevant to its tap water, so that path first needs a per-city water-source-type lookup (e.g. via EPA SDWIS) before it could be used correctly. Real project if ever pursued, not a quick fix. Low coverage (~5-15%) is accepted as correct: the chart-group fallback (`homes_by_decade`, real per-city Census data, same group) silently covers every city this chart can't, so no page is ever left without a chart.
